---
title: "Reproducibility repositories"
subtitle: "Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, the code forges, and the Open Science Framework after 2026"
---

This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) is about the other end of the data exchange from the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd): not where data are obtained, but where a finished piece of work is deposited so that another person can find it, cite it and re-run it. It sets out what a repository has to do, compares the general-purpose repositories that researchers actually use, and then gives the Open Science Framework (OSF) the long treatment, because the course's own materials live there, because the preregistration you write in Part 4 is modelled on an OSF registration, and because the OSF is changing shape at the end of 2026 in a way that anyone learning it now has to know about. The closing sections keep what the shorter version of this module carried before: the course's own trail on the OSF, the vocabulary of registrations and forks, and the preregistration templates.

The module assumes no more than the workshop itself does. It is a natural companion to the [git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd), which is about keeping a history of your own work and collaborating on it, and to the data sources module, which is about the archives at the start of the pipeline. Where the three overlap, as they do at the UK Data Service, which distributes the national surveys and also takes deposits of project data, or at GitHub, which is both a working tool and a place where code is found, the overlap is pointed out rather than hidden.

## 1. What a repository does {#sec-what}

A folder on a laptop, a departmental server and a link in a paper's appendix all fail the same test: they do not survive the person who made them. A repository in the sense meant here does six things that those do not, and the six are the checklist for choosing one.

- **A persistent identifier.** A DOI (digital object identifier) or an equivalent that resolves to the deposit for as long as the repository exists, and that a paper can cite. Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare and the OSF all mint DOIs; a GitHub repository does not.
- **Versioning.** A new version gets a new identifier while the old one still resolves, so a reader who followed the citation in a 2027 paper gets what the 2027 paper used.
- **A licence.** A statement, attached to the deposit, of what others may do with it. CC BY 4.0 is the common choice for data and text, and an open-source licence such as MIT or GPL for code; the licence that the underlying data carry limits what you may deposit at all, as the course's own GESIS-derived data illustrate.
- **Metadata.** A title, creators, description, keywords, related identifiers and dates, in a form that indexes and catalogues can read. The quality of the metadata decides whether anyone finds the deposit who was not sent the link.
- **Preservation.** A commitment, usually institutional, to keep the files readable over decades, sometimes certified (the CoreTrustSeal is the certification most social-science archives hold).
- **Access control.** Public by default, with the possibility of an embargo, a restricted file that is applied for, or a private deposit that only a reviewer can reach through a link.

Repositories come in four kinds, and the Center for Open Science's own guidance, written for researchers moving off OSF projects, sorts them in the same way: discipline-specific archives (the UK Data Service, GESIS, ICPSR, the Qualitative Data Repository), generalist repositories (Zenodo, Figshare, Dataverse, Dryad), institutional repositories run by universities, and journal-based repositories attached to a publisher. The same guidance gives a first step that is worth repeating: "Talk to your institutional librarian about who should host your data and other research outputs." Funders and journals increasingly require a named repository, and the ESRC's requirement that funded data be offered to the UK Data Service is the local instance of that.

## 2. The generalist repositories {#sec-generalist}

| Repository | What it takes | Identifier and versions | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/)** | Any research output: data, code, materials, slides, reports | A DOI per version and a concept DOI for all versions | Free, hosted by CERN | Records can be linked to one another as parts of a whole; a GitHub repository can be set to archive each release automatically, which is the standard way of giving code a DOI |
| **[Harvard Dataverse](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/)** and the other Dataverse installations | Datasets with their documentation; collections nest, so a project can be a collection with datasets inside it | A DOI per dataset, with versions | Free at Harvard; institutional installations elsewhere | File-level embargo and restricted access; the `dataverse` R package uploads and downloads by DOI |
| **[Figshare](https://figshare.com/)** | Datasets, code, figures, presentations, posters | A DOI per item and version | Free for individuals; many universities run their own instance | Quick to use; the institutional instances are often the university repository in disguise |
| **[Dryad](https://datadryad.org/)** | Data accompanying a journal article, curated | A DOI | A data publishing charge, often paid by the journal or the institution | Curation is what you pay for |
| **[UK Data Service ReShare](https://reshare.ukdataservice.ac.uk/)** | Research data from UK projects, in particular ESRC-funded ones | A persistent identifier and a catalogue record | Free | The route that satisfies the ESRC's data policy; the data become part of the national collection and inherit its access tiers |
| **ICPSR (openICPSR)** | Social and behavioural science data, self-deposited or curated | A DOI | Self-deposit free; curation priced | The US counterpart of ReShare |
| **[Qualitative Data Repository](https://qdr.syr.edu/)** | Qualitative and multi-method data, with the ethics handled | A DOI | Deposit fees, quoted by COS at $750 to $2,500 | The one place that takes interview and fieldwork data seriously |
| **The Open Science Framework** | Registrations and preprints; until February 2027, projects holding anything | A DOI for public registrations and, on request, for projects | Free | See [section 4](#sec-osf) |

The comparison rows are drawn from the COS guide on [choosing a repository](https://help.osf.io/article/735-choosing-a-repository), read on 8 September 2026, and from the repositories' own pages. Which one to use depends on what the deposit is. A dataset that other people should find and reuse goes to the disciplinary archive if there is one (the UK Data Service for a UK project) and to Dataverse or Zenodo otherwise. Code goes to a forge (the next section) with each release archived on Zenodo. A finished report, a set of slides, a preprint of a paper: Zenodo or Figshare, or the preprint server of your field.

## 3. Code forges {#sec-forges}

[GitHub](https://github.com/), [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/), [Codeberg](https://codeberg.org/) and the self-hosted Forgejo are *forges*: services that host git repositories with an issue tracker, pull requests, wikis and, in GitHub's and GitLab's case, a great deal else, from continuous integration to website hosting. They are where code is written, reviewed and collaborated on, and the [git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd) is about using them for that. They are also where most research code is found, which makes them look like repositories in the sense of this page. They are not. A GitHub repository has no DOI, can be renamed, transferred or deleted by its owner in a minute, and carries no commitment to preservation. The remedy is cheap and standard: tag a release on the forge and let Zenodo archive it, which gives the release a DOI that the paper cites while the forge keeps the living copy. Every published version of the course's own workspace is meant to travel that way.

## 4. The Open Science Framework, and what is changing {#sec-osf}

The OSF, run by the non-profit Center for Open Science (COS), has been the general-purpose repository behind almost everything that this course touches. Its help pages describe an OSF **project** as "[a flexible, collaborative workspace where researchers can plan, manage, and share any part of their research lifecycle](https://help.osf.io/article/253-project-structure)", and a **component** as an "[optional sub-project nested within a parent project ... used to break a large project into smaller parts](https://help.osf.io/article/253-project-structure)". Projects and components form a tree; each node carries files, a wiki, contributors, storage add-ons that connect to Google Drive or Dropbox or GitHub, and its own privacy setting; a project can be forked, registered, given a DOI, and linked to a preprint. That is the OSF that the literature of the last decade refers to, and that the three nodes behind this course were built on.

### 4.1 The transition {#sec-transition}

On 27 August 2026 COS announced that OSF Projects are being phased out, and the help pages set out the timetable. The reason given is financial: keeping the projects workflow running "would require COS to raise approximately $4-5 million each year for the next several years", which the organisation cannot sustain, so the OSF is being narrowed to the parts where it can do most. Two dates matter.

- **From 16 November 2026**, "no new projects or child components of existing projects can be created on OSF. All other functions remain the same." Existing projects can still be edited, files added, contributors changed, until the second date.
- **From 19 February 2027**, "all OSF projects will be converted into a read-only project." Content stays viewable and downloadable at the same URLs and DOIs, an administrator can still delete a project or make a private one public, but nothing can be edited, added or uploaded, no new component or fork can be made, and a public project cannot be made private again. Private projects stay available to the people who already have access, and COS says it will give at least twelve months' notice before removing any of them.

What is **not** changing is stated just as plainly. "Registrations & Preregistrations and Preprints are unaffected by this change": both workflows continue, new registrations can be created, and the community-run preprint servers hosted on OSF Preprints keep running (the generalist OSF Preprints server itself has been closed to new submissions since 25 August 2025, with the existing preprints kept). Public projects remain "accessible indefinitely as read-only records", their DOIs "continue to resolve indefinitely", and OSF Search still finds them. COS's own summary of what the OSF becomes is worth quoting: "a free, open-source platform for creating and linking transparent research records", built around registrations, preprints and links to outputs held elsewhere. The FAQs add that the registration and preprint workflows "are not meant as replacements for Project storage", and that "Registrations are designed to document and share preregistrations, study plans, and similar practices. You should identify a data repository for sharing data, materials, and other supplements."

For someone with an existing project, the guidance is to do nothing if the project is a finished public record: "If your public Project does not need further updates, we strongly recommend that you take no action", because moving a deposit that already has a DOI risks a second DOI for the same work and a split citation record. An active project should be moved to a repository suited to its content before February 2027, with the OSF's DOI or URL redirected to the new home through the [redirect request](https://help.osf.io/article/750-redirect-my-doi-or-url), which only an administrator of the project can submit. A private project should be exported or made public. The COS guide on [replicating a project structure](https://help.osf.io/article/749-replicate-your-project-structure-in-other-repositories) maps the OSF tree onto the alternatives: on Zenodo, one record for the former top-level project and one for each substantive component, linked through the "Related works" fields as parts of a whole; on Dataverse, a collection for the project with a child collection for each component and a dataset for each folder.

### 4.2 Working on the OSF from 2027 {#sec-osf-2027}

The practical shape of the platform for a new piece of work is therefore this. The **registration** is the record: a frozen, time-stamped document of the plan, created directly on OSF Registries without a project behind it, using one of the templates (the standard OSF Preregistration, the AsPredicted form, the secondary-data template and a dozen others), kept private under an embargo of up to four years if need be, and given a DOI the moment it is public. Files can be uploaded as part of the submission, within a 5 GB limit, but that is not where the data live. The data, the code and the materials live in a repository of the kinds described above, and the registration's **Resources** fields carry their DOIs, which is also what earns a registration its open-practice badges for data, code and materials. A **preprint** on one of the community servers can point at the same DOIs. The OSF holds the plan and the links; the deposits are elsewhere. That arrangement is what a registration was always for, and the transition makes it the only arrangement.

## 5. The course's own trail on the OSF {#sec-trail}

Three nodes in the OSF tree carry the materials of the EU-frames case, and all three are public projects, which means that from 19 February 2027 they are read-only records at the same addresses.

**[`osf.io/8rtwe`](https://osf.io/8rtwe/) – the official Multi100 archival record.** The component that the Multi100 project preserved for analyst C6HJR: the materials exactly as submitted, frozen and citable. The transition changes nothing about it; it was already an archive in the strict sense.

**[`osf.io/6zqct`](https://osf.io/6zqct/) – the analyst's maintained fork, and the fetch target of the course.** OSF describes this node as "a public fork" of `8rtwe`, maintained by the facilitator for teaching. It carries a later revision of the analysis script and its exported dataset, revised Task 1 and Task 2 documents, and `EUframes_cy.csv` in its main folder, which is what the workspace's `R/get_data.R` fetches. After February 2027 it can no longer take a new file, so the maintained copy of the workspace from then on is the [`replication-lab`](https://github.com/CodeMoreh/replication-lab) repository on GitHub, whose releases are the versions to cite, and the fork on OSF stands as the record of the materials up to that date.

**[`osf.io/h7432`](https://osf.io/h7432/) – the full SCORE dossier, one paper put through all three Rs.** The parent node under which the whole reproducibility apparatus around the case sits, with one component per check.

| Component | What | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `whp4b` | Original materials collected by the Center for Open Science | View-only |
| `cf8en` | Author-provided code – two Stata do-files, supplied on request; the original author's own statement records that the data cannot be forwarded and must come from GESIS | Code available, data restricted |
| `8fwrt` | Power analysis for the replication | – |
| `ezhcs` | **Push-button reproduction**, run with the original author's own code | **Failed.** "The authors used file names that did not correspond with the names of the files available for download. Additionally 16 datasets are listed on the website as being used but the code references 18 files." |
| `4rjbf` | **Source-data reproduction** | **'Not reproduced'** – the effect size "could not be extract[ed] nor re-calculate[d]" from the source data |
| `gr8u6` | **Multi100 robustness** – five independent reanalysts, including analyst C6HJR whose materials this course reanalyses | All five coefficients negative; partial r from −0.006 to −0.452 |
| `zt5y2` | **Secondary-data replication** – fresh Eurobarometer and Eurostat waves, preregistered, N = 352,114 person-year observations | **Not replicated – sign flip.** "We found a positive coefficient for unemployment on cosmopolitan framing": b = +0.002, p = .046 |

That table is what a well-kept repository record lets a reader establish without emailing anyone: a push-button check that failed for a checkable reason, file names that did not match the files; a source-data check on which the reported effect could not be recovered; a robustness check that held the direction while the size moved by a factor of roughly 75; and a replication on new data that flipped the sign. Each verdict is legible because the materials sit in a public tree rather than in a folder on someone's laptop, and the read-only status that the tree acquires in 2027 does not make it less legible. It does mean that a project that expects to keep moving, as this course does, needs a living copy elsewhere with the frozen record pointing at it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Open [`osf.io/h7432`](https://osf.io/h7432/) and find the `zt5y2` component in the table above. Locate the sentence reporting the sign-flipped coefficient in the materials of that component, and note the exact figures: the coefficient, its standard error, and the significance level. This is the scavenger task that the in-session OSF segment sets in Part 4, and the page will look the same after February 2027; what will have changed is that nobody can add to it.
:::

## 6. Registrations, forks and archives {#sec-registration}

Three pieces of vocabulary from the OSF are needed for the rest of this module, and all three survive the transition, one of them in changed form.

A **registration** is "[a frozen version of your project that can never be edited or deleted, but you can issue a withdrawal of it later](https://help.osf.io/article/330-registrations)", time-stamped and given its own permanent identifier. This is the mechanism behind preregistration: it captures a study plan before the data are seen, or, for a reanalysis of existing data, before the specific analytical choices are made, so that the plan cannot later be quietly rewritten to fit the result. A public registration receives a DOI automatically; an embargoed one stays private for up to four years; a registration can be updated through a transparent update that records what changed and why, and withdrawn, which removes its contents but keeps the metadata and the justification. The Multi100 reanalysts worked from a registered protocol of this kind, which is why their five results can be compared on equal footing, and from 2027 a registration is created directly on OSF Registries rather than from a project.

A **fork**, in the git sense that the [git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd#sec-github) uses, is your own editable copy of someone else's repository, kept separate so that you can change it without touching the original. The OSF had the same operation for projects, and "a public fork" is what OSF calls `osf.io/6zqct`; after 19 February 2027 no new fork can be made on the OSF, so the manoeuvre lives on in the forges alone.

An **archive** freezes materials and a **registration** freezes a plan, and the difference is what allows the date of a plan to be compared with the date of a result. The archival record at `8rtwe` and the Multi100 protocol are the two halves of that comparison for this case.

## 7. Preregistration templates {#sec-prereg-templates}

The earlier sections were about materials that other people deposited and a plan that the Multi100 team registered in advance. This section is about writing your own, because Part 4 of the workshop asks you to do just that: complete a preregistration block in your own report before you run your chosen specification.

An OSF registration is the general mechanism. What varies between registrations is the **template**, the fixed set of questions that a researcher answers before the data are touched. OSF Registries hosts more than a dozen, built for different kinds of study, and two are worth knowing by name.

**The AsPredicted-style short template.** Built by the team behind [AsPredicted.org](https://aspredicted.org/) and available as one of the registration forms on OSF, this is the simplest entry point and the one recommended for the in-session exercise. It asks a short, fixed sequence of questions, the hypotheses, the key variables and analysis, how the sample will be determined, and what would count as excluding data, each answered in a sentence or two rather than a full protocol. Its appeal for a workshop is its brevity: a participant with no preregistration experience can complete it in the time that Part 4 sets aside, and what it demands, stating the analysis before running it in a form specific enough that it cannot be reinterpreted afterwards, is what a longer template demands too.

**The secondary-data template (van den Akker and colleagues).** A short-form template written for a study whose data have not yet been collected assumes something that is not true of this course: that the researcher has not yet seen the data. A reanalysis of an existing public dataset breaks that assumption from the outset. You can see summary statistics, published tables and other researchers' results before you commit to a specification of your own. Van den Akker and colleagues' template is built around that difference. Where a fresh-data template asks what you will collect and how, a secondary-data template asks what you have already seen and what you have not: which parts of the dataset or its published results you have been exposed to, whether your hypothesis was formed before or after that exposure, and what remains genuinely undetermined about your analytical choices at the point of writing the plan. For a Multi100-style robustness reanalysis this is the more accurate match for what preregistration can promise: not that you approached the data blind, but that your specific choices were fixed and dated before you ran them.

**How the course block maps onto these.** The block you complete in Part 4 has the structure of the AsPredicted form, a small number of short and specific questions, adapted for a specification-menu reanalysis rather than a fresh study. Instead of a hypothesis and a test, it asks you to state your chosen specification, one option from each Level 1 choice and the Level 2 and 3 settings you keep, and to justify it against the estimand and the graph you built earlier in the day. It is deliberately the lighter of the two templates, because the Part 4 time budget favours a form that can be completed and rendered inside a defined slot. The secondary-data template is the take-home reading for anyone who wants to see how the same discipline scales up to a plan detailed enough to submit as a real registration.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Read the question list of the AsPredicted template at [aspredicted.org](https://aspredicted.org/) and, separately, skim the structure of the secondary-data template. For a single specification you might choose from the [specification menu](../exercise/spec-menu.qmd), say the positive composite as outcome, the raw unemployment rate, two-way fixed effects, all years, no weights, write one sentence answering the central question of the secondary-data template in your own words: what, if anything, had you already seen of the results on this claim before settling on that specification? A truthful answer to that question, written down before anything runs, is what separates a preregistration that constrains you from one that only decorates a result you had already half-decided on.
:::

## 8. Depositing a reanalysis of your own {#sec-deposit}

Put together, the sections above give a route for a reanalysis like the one you build on the day, written so that it works after the OSF transition as well as before it.

1. **The code lives on a forge.** Put the report, the scripts and the codebook in a git repository on GitHub or an equivalent, with a licence file and a README that says what the repository is and how to render it. The [git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd) takes you from nothing to that point.
2. **Each version is archived with a DOI.** Tag a release on the forge and let Zenodo archive it, so that the version you cite in a paper is the version a reader gets. The concept DOI covers all versions; the version DOI is the one for the paper.
3. **The data go where their licence allows.** Derived aggregates that you are free to share go with the code or into Dataverse or ReShare with a citation of their sources; licensed microdata, such as the Eurobarometer files, never leave your machine, and the README says how a reader obtains them from the archive, which is what the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) sets out for this case.
4. **The plan goes on the OSF.** Create the registration on OSF Registries before the analysis runs, with the secondary-data template or the AsPredicted form, and put the DOIs from steps 2 and 3 into its Resources fields. Keep the embargo short or none at all.
5. **The report is part of the release.** Render it to HTML or PDF and include the rendered file in the tagged release, so that the numbers a reader sees are the ones the code produced on the day you released it.
6. **Cite the data sources properly.** The archive's own citation for each survey wave and indicator, with the download dates, in the report and in the repository metadata.

A reanalysis deposited that way has a public plan with a date, a public record of the code and results with a version, and a stated route to the data it cannot carry. That is what the SCORE checks in section 5 needed from the original paper and did not always find.
